sharedText: and they shall hear my voice ... that there may be one fold, and one shepherd
reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter and a correct identification — 'one fold, and one shepherd' is a KJV singleton and it is reproduced intact. It is excluded here only because the chapter's use of John 10:16 is adjudicated two verses earlier, at 16:1, where the borrowing does something the machine cannot see: 'not of this fold' is rewritten as 'not of this land'. 16:3 restores the metaphor 16:1 dismantled, and the two verses are one movement. The reader who arrives at 16:3 should be sent to 16:1, and to 3 Nephi 15:17 and 15:21, where the same verse is quoted verbatim twice in the preceding chapter.

A five-word run of pure command formula. John 15:17 is 'These things I command you, that ye love one another'; 3 Nephi 16:4 is 'And I command you that ye shall write these sayings'. Nothing is shared but the syntax of issuing an order, and the Book of Mormon uses that syntax continuously. Recorded rather than passed over in silence because this verse does carry a genuine Johannine borrowing — John 16:23's 'ask the Father in my name' — and a reader could reasonably suppose the two were connected. They are not; the John 15 candidate is boilerplate and the John 16 one is a KJV singleton.

The run straddles a clause boundary and joins two unrelated phrases: 'scattered forth upon the face of the earth' + 'because of their unbelief'. Jeremiah 15:4 has 'removed into all kingdoms of the earth, because of Manasseh'. The scattering is a real thematic overlap, but the KJV's own verse for it in this chapter's argument is Leviticus 26:33 ('I will scatter you among the heathen'), which stands behind 16:8-11 and is adjudicated at 16:11, and the 'because of' clause belongs to Romans 11:20, adjudicated at 16:4 itself. The Jeremiah row is the machine finding a boundary.

sharedText: the four quarters of the earth
reason: A KJV singleton and a real borrowing, adjudicated for this book at 3 Nephi 5:24, where the mediation test against Isaiah 11:12 is run and the choice of 'quarters' over Isaiah's 'corners' is shown to be decisive. 16:5 is Christ's own use of a phrase Mormon has already used as narrator eleven chapters earlier, in the same gathering sense and with the same reversal of Revelation's meaning — Revelation's four quarters are where Gog and Magog are gathered from to make war, the Book of Mormon's are where Israel is gathered from to be given a covenant. Nothing is added here that 5:24 does not already carry, and the standing exclusion at 3 Nephi 5:26 covers the same candidate.

The wrong half of the phrase, for the reason already given in the register at 3 Nephi 5:26: Jeremiah 49:36 reads 'the four quarters of heaven', not of the earth, and its winds scatter Elam rather than gather anyone. 3 Nephi 16:5 reads 'of the earth' and gathers. Repeated here because the machine ranks it afresh at every occurrence of the phrase and a reader arriving at this verse has not necessarily seen the entry at 5:26.

This is the register's most interesting entry in the chapter and it has to be declined. 'Trodden under feet' — with the plural — occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 14:19 and Isaiah 28:3, against five for the singular 'trodden under foot'. 3 Nephi 16:8 has the plural, and both 1830 and 1920 read 'trodden under feet' there, so it is not an orthographic accident of the first edition. Seven verses later, at 16:15, the same book has the singular, 'trodden under foot', because it is quoting Matthew 5:13. The chapter therefore distinguishes the two KJV forms and uses each in a passage where that form is at home, which is the kind of fact that ordinarily makes a link. It does not make one here. Isaiah 28:3's plural belongs to 'the crown of pride, the drunkards of Ephraim' — the trodden party is Israel's own northern kingdom, undone by drink, and there is no Gentile in the verse. 3 Nephi 16:8's trodden party is Israel scattered by Gentiles who have 'come forth upon the face of this land'. Three words, opposed agents, and no second point of contact anywhere in Isaiah 28. What survives is worth recording without the link: whoever wrote 16:8 and 16:15 had both King James spellings available and did not mix them.

Ranked at both 16:8 and 16:9, and 'come out from among them' is a KJV singleton, so the temptation is real — the more so because 2 Corinthians 6:17 is itself a citation of Isaiah 52:11, three verses past the block this chapter quotes at 16:18-20. The senses are opposed at the only point that matters. Paul's imperative is voluntary and self-protective: the believers are told to separate themselves from unbelievers, 'be ye separate, and touch not the unclean thing', and the promise attached is 'I will receive you'. 3 Nephi 16:8-9 is involuntary and punitive: the house of Israel 'have been cast out from among them, and have been trodden under feet by them'. One party leaves to stay clean; the other is expelled and trampled. Note also that the matching words are not the KJV's Isaiah at all — Isaiah 52:11 reads 'Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence' — so the phrase that produces the candidate is Paul's own rendering, and the Isaiah 52 adjacency, however striking, cannot be used to support the row. The genuine source of 16:9's clause is 1 Kings 9:7's 'will I cast out of my sight', adjudicated there.

A five-word run inside a list of passive infinitives — 'to be smitten, and to be afflicted, and to be slain, and to be cast out' — where the shared material is the list's grammar. Esther 7:4's 'to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish' is the same construction and no more. Esther is pleading for the Jews before Ahasuerus and the verse turns on being sold; 3 Nephi 16:9 is God rehearsing what he has caused to be done to his own people. The list's real background is the covenant curse of Leviticus 26, which the following verses take up explicitly at 16:11.

Five words of which four are function words. 'The mercies of the LORD' in Psalm 89:1 is the opening of a psalm of praise; 'the mercies of the Father unto the Gentiles' in 3 Nephi 16:9 is one term in a balanced pair with 'the judgements of the Father upon my people'. The pairing of mercy and judgement is the verse's real structure and it is not Psalm 89's.

Genuinely close in subject — Jeremiah 12:14 is God plucking his people out of their land because of evil neighbours — and still too little. The shared words are a first-person causative and the phrase 'my people', both of which the Book of Mormon uses constantly and this chapter uses six times. Jeremiah's clause is 'the inheritance which I have caused my people Israel to inherit', a possession; 3 Nephi 16:9's is 'I have caused my people ... to be smitten', an affliction. The verb's object is opposite in kind.

'The whole earth' occurs in twenty-eight KJV verses and the rest of the run is connective. Daniel 7:23's fourth beast devours the whole earth and treads it down; 3 Nephi 16:10's Gentiles are lifted up 'above all the people of the whole earth'. Devouring the earth and being exalted above its people are different claims, and Daniel supplies no other word here. The verse's real intertext is Romans 11:21-22, which is where the row is written, at moderate and with a stated whyNot.

A five-word KJV singleton, which is ordinarily the strongest evidence this catalogue can produce, and it is worthless here. Revelation 17:1 is one of the seven vial-angels summoning John: 'Come hither; I will shew unto thee the judgment of the great whore that sitteth upon many waters.' 3 Nephi 16:12 is the Father addressing the house of Israel: 'I will shew unto thee, O house of Israel, that the Gentiles shall not have power over you.' The speaker, the addressee and the thing shown are all different, and nothing else of Revelation 17 is anywhere near. The phrase is simply the King James formula for one party undertaking to show another something, and its being a singleton is arithmetic rather than significance — compare the standing entry at Helaman 1:1. The 1830 spelling 'shew', which 1920 modernized to 'show', is worth recording as KJV orthography surviving in the first edition, but it attests the translation's general idiom and not this verse.

'Hearken unto my voice' is one of the King James Bible's commonest covenant formulas and 'hear my voice' alone occurs in eleven verses. Exodus 18:19 is Jethro offering Moses administrative advice; 3 Nephi 16:15 is God stating the condition on which he will let Israel tread the Gentiles down. The verse's actual borrowing, seventeen consecutive words of Matthew 5:13, sits immediately after this run and is adjudicated at the verse.

sharedText: for the Lord hath comforted his people
reason: A genuine seven-word agreement, and displaced. 'Hath comforted his people' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 49:13 and Isaiah 52:9, so the clause alone cannot choose between them — but the rest of 3 Nephi 16:19 decides it without ambiguity. The Book of Mormon reads 'Break forth into joy, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem ... he hath redeemed Jerusalem'; Isaiah 49:13 reads 'break forth into singing, O mountains ... and will have mercy upon his afflicted'. 'Break forth into joy' and 'waste places of Jerusalem' are each KJV singletons and each belongs to 52:9. The candidate is recorded because Isaiah 49 is quoted at length elsewhere in the Book of Mormon (1 Nephi 21, 2 Nephi 6), so a reader has reason to expect it here, and because the two verses are close enough that the machine cannot separate them.
